reasoning: The option to buy add-on tokens at $1.25 per 1M is about 40% below the low end of the $2.10-$2.40 SSP range, an incremental discount the customer would not get without this contract, so it is a material right (606-10-55-41 to 55-42), as in rr-f1-01.
10% off the $2.60 list price is $2.34 per 1M, inside the $2.10-$2.40 SSP range, so the option gives no incremental discount and is not a material right (606-10-55-43), as in rr-f1-02.
doubts: The price is fixed off the list price at the Effective Date for three years. If list price and SSP rise during the term, the locked price could fall below SSP later, but the material-right test is made at inception, so no label.

reasoning: Annual expiry of unused tokens matches the vendor's standard order form, so there is no departure to review. Unused prepaid tokens raise breakage (606-10-55-46 to 55-49), which has no label (decision #007, families T4); the fee is fixed and non-refundable, so no variable consideration or refund right.

Despite the 'preferred rate' wording, $2.30 per 1M sits inside the $2.10-$2.40 SSP range, so the option conveys no incremental discount and no material right (606-10-55-43). Below list price is not the test; SSP is.

The $2.25 tier is within SSP, but the right to buy tokens at $0.80 per 1M after 500B of add-ons a year is 62% below the SSP low end and 56% below the $1.80 standard volume floor, a discount similar customers don't get, so it is likely a material right (606-10-55-42), following rr-f1-04.
doubts: Whether the right is material depends on how likely the customer is to exceed 500B of add-on purchases in a contract year; that does not change the need for review.

reasoning: The standard terms deem acceptance on delivery with repair-or-replace only; this clause lets the customer return the software for a full $750,000 refund if acceptance criteria aren't met in 60 days, a refund right that puts the fee at risk (606-10-55-22 to 55-27) and, under decision #007, variable consideration (606-10-32-6).
doubts: The bigger accounting question is customer acceptance and when control transfers (606-10-55-85 to 55-88): if the Exhibit B criteria are not objectively verifiable, revenue may wait for acceptance. None of the six labels captures that, and the criteria aren't in the case.

reasoning: Look-alike: a standard non-refundable-fees clause. It grants no refund, credit, or cancellation right; it removes one, so no consideration applies and nothing departs from standard terms.

SLA credits are variable consideration in substance (606-10-32-6), but this SLA matches the stated standard: credits only, on request, capped at 15% of the monthly fee. It is handled at the policy level, so no deal review (decision #004, rr-f2-03).

The standard SLA gives credits only; paying unused credits in cash at the end of the term turns them into a cash refund liability that can't lapse. That departs from standard in a way that changes the variable consideration estimate (606-10-32-6) and, under decision #007, is also a refund right.
doubts: The amount at stake is still capped by the 10% SLA, so the dollar effect may be small; the trigger rests on the change from credit to cash, as in rr-f2-02.

reasoning: A $150,000 success fee contingent on the customer's cost per ticket falling 20% is a performance bonus, variable consideration to estimate and likely constrain because the outcome depends on factors outside the vendor's control (606-10-32-6, 32-11 to 32-12). It is not a refund, so no refund_return.
doubts: The case states the vendor's standard SLA but not that its standard pricing has no performance-based fees (lesson 010). The trigger assumes a success fee is non-standard, which seems safe, and a contingent fee of this size needs a deal-level estimate anyway.

reasoning: Net 90 is customary for the vendor's Japan customers, and payment lands about 90 days into each service year, so no gap between service and payment exceeds about 9 months. The one-year practical expedient applies (606-10-32-18), as in rr-f3-01.

The practical expedient doesn't apply, so the vendor must assess a significant financing component (606-10-32-15 to 32-20), as in rr-f3-03.
doubts: Extended payment on a license delivered up front can also raise collectibility and implied price concession questions (606-10-25-1(e), 32-7(b)), not labelled here. The deal field 'subscription' holds a perpetual license, a field-name quirk.

reasoning: Quarterly invoicing in advance on net 30 matches the vendor's North American payment terms, and payment is never more than about 2 months from the service it covers, so the practical expedient applies (606-10-32-18). No financing component and nothing to review.
doubts: The vendor's standard billing frequency (for example, annual in advance) isn't stated, only its payment terms. Quarterly billing has no revenue effect either way, so the label holds.

reasoning: Prepaying the full $1,200,000 at signing means the last month of service follows payment by about 23 months, so the one-year practical expedient doesn't apply and the vendor must assess a significant financing component (606-10-32-15 to 32-20). doubts: The trigger rests on the over-a-year gap; the case doesn't state the vendor's standard billing frequency, so 'departs from standard' depends on assuming multi-year prepayment isn't standard.

reasoning: Invoicing the whole $360,000 at the end of the term, payable net 60, departs from net 30 and leaves the first months of service unpaid for about 13 months, so the one-year practical expedient isn't clearly available and the vendor must assess financing (606-10-32-15 to 32-18).
doubts: The gap exceeds a year only for the first month or so; the average gap is about 8 months and the financing effect is likely insignificant. reasoning: The Prior Order ends 6 months early and its $500,000 of unused prepaid value carries into a new, larger order, a contract modification (606-10-25-10). doubts: `computed` doesn't state the new order's per-token price ($1.90 per 1M, 5% below the SSP low end), although other F4 cases compute price vs SSP. It doesn't change the labels.

reasoning: Look-alike: an amendment that only updates the billing address and invoice contact. It changes neither scope nor price, so it is not a contract modification under 606-10-25-10, and nothing else applies.

The customer exercises an option already in the Prior Order (Section 4.2) at $2.10 per 1M, inside the SSP range. An option at SSP is not a material right, and its exercise is an optional purchase accounted for as a new contract when exercised (606-10-55-42 to 55-43). No change to the existing contract's enforceable rights needed approval, so it is not a modification, and the existing accounting is unchanged.
doubts: Some reviewers would label contract_modification by analogy to rr-f4-03, since scope and price rise. I distinguish them: rr-f4-03 had no add-on option, so the parties approved a new change; here the right was already enforceable. Either way the accounting is a separate contract at SSP, so the trigger is false.

reasoning: A blend-and-extend: the price for the remaining 6 months drops from $2.00 to $1.80 per 1M (a $100,000 credit) and the term extends 12 months at $1.80 per 1M, 10% below the SSP low end. That is an approved change in price and scope (606-10-25-10), not priced at SSP, so it's likely prospective under 606-10-25-13(a) (see 32-45).
doubts: The $100,000 reduction could be read as a price concession (variable_consideration, 606-10-32-7(b)) if it was granted for past performance issues or was expected at inception (families T8). Nothing in the case suggests that, so I labelled the modification only. The extension is committed, not optional, so no material right.

reasoning: Self-describing clause: it calls itself independent, but it adds 300B tokens co-terminous with the Prior Order, approved by the same parties, which in substance is a change in scope and price (606-10-25-10).
